title: The tornaviaje: to sail back from Asia, you had to head north
cover:
They could go.
Nobody could get back.

scenes.text: In 1521, Spain already knew how to cross the Pacific. What nobody knew… was how to get back.
The culprit: the wind. In the tropics, the trade winds always blow west. Sailing back that way was like walking up a down escalator.
For more than forty years, everyone who tried it failed.
Until 1565, when the friar Andrés de Urdaneta did something that seemed absurd: to go east, he headed north.
He climbed to the 39th parallel, level with Japan. Up there the wind blows the other way, and the Kuroshio current pushes toward America.
He left Cebu on June 1st. Four months later, he reached Acapulco.

That route, the tornaviaje, was sailed by the Manila Galleon for 250 years: American silver for Chinese silk and porcelain. According to historians Flynn and Giráldez, that is how global trade was born.
Share it with someone who thinks globalization is a modern invention.
